verified_record.age_estimate: documented only as "centenaria" (very old); no numeric age given by any source

location.address: In the meadow of the Etxeita farmhouse, opposite the Santa Kataliñe/Santa Catalina hermitage, off the BI-3341 road between Goiuria (Iurreta) and Garai, Garai, Bizkaia
location.neighbourhood: Etxeita caserio grounds, Garai (Durangaldea district), Bizkaia

verified_record.access: Free but on working farmland: from the Santa Catalina/Santa Kataliñe hermitage on the BI-3341 between Goiuria and Garai, a paved track crosses about 800m of pine wood to the Etxeita farmhouse; the tree stands in the meadow just north of the farm buildings. The official Bizkaia government listing notes an information panel stands at the tree, and a Basque tourism site (MugaKultura, Oct 2025) gives these exact directions and actively invites visitors, while asking them to respect the place and the people who live there. Flagging for a future access check (e.g. OSM path tags) rather than treating the farmhouse setting as settled.
verified_record.transport: Rural Durangaldea, Bizkaia; no public transport reaches the farm track. Garai and neighbouring Iurreta are about 26km from Bilbao (which we already publish); a car is the realistic way to reach it.
verified_record.verify_notes:
THREE SOURCES, well past the two-source bar: (1) bizkaia.eus, the Diputacion Foral de Bizkaia's own official monumental-tree register page, listing this as Natural Monument 'Encina de Garai (ES213002)', species 'Quercus ilex ilex', with coordinates Lat 43.19801828 / Long -2.62562536 (matches this lead's coordinate, 43.197819/-2.625761, to within a few metres, so location_precision is confirmed on the register's own tree-level coordinate); (2) es.wikipedia.org's 'Arboles singulares de la Comunidad Autonoma del Pais Vasco' article, an independent encyclopedia entry with its own description and citations; (3) mugakultura.eus, a Basque local-culture/tourism site's article dated 2025-10-23 (fetched and read directly, not taken from a search summary), marking the tree's 30th anniversary of protection and confirming it is still standing and actively promoted as a place to visit AS OF LATE 2025, which is good recent alive-evidence.

DESIGNATION: protected since 1995 under Decreto 265/1995 (Gobierno Vasco), one of the Basque Country's first legally protected singular trees; it automatically became a legal 'monumento natural' under later Basque conservation law per the bizkaia.eus page's own text.

DIMENSIONS: the bizkaia.eus register gives an actual TRUNK figure, not a search-summary guess: 5.7m perimeter measured at 1.3m height (girth_cm 570 above is this measured figure, not derived), stem/bole height 0.8m, total height 8.5m, crown diameter 20m. Wikipedia and MugaKultura both separately describe the CROWN (not the trunk) as having a circumference of 'more than 60 metres' and a diameter of 'more than 19 metres', consistent with the register's 20m crown-diameter figure; do not let the writer confuse the ~60m CROWN circumference with the tree's actual 5.7m TRUNK girth, they describe different things.

AGE: no source anywhere gives a number. Wikipedia's generic list labels it 'Centenario' (i.e. very old, unspecified) and MugaKultura calls it 'esta encina centenaria'; both are vague and I kept them vague per the rule rather than inventing a figure. Recorded age_min/age_max as null (empty) rather than guessing from girth, because I have no published Quercus ilex growth-rate figure to derive from and the sources themselves decline to give a number; a reader with local knowledge or a dendrologist could answer this on the page.

STORY MATERIAL: shaped by generations of pruning to feed livestock on its acorns, which gave it the wide symmetrical crown; oral tradition says a flock of up to 360 sheep has sheltered under it. Views over the Durangaldea mountains from the meadow.

ACCESS, the genuinely open question: the tree stands on the grounds of a still-working, apparently inhabited farmhouse (Etxeita). This is NOT a doorbell-and-permission case (no source describes needing to ask anyone, there is a marked track and an official information panel, and a tourism site actively gives turn-by-turn directions and encourages the visit), but it is also not an unambiguous public park either, and the tourism piece explicitly asks visitors to be respectful of the people living there. I am delivering this per 'publish what verifies, the access call gets an honest caveat rather than a hold', flagging it so a later pass can settle it further with an OSM foot/access tag check on the BI-3341-to-Etxeita track (the Ypres technique), which I did not have time for in this pass.

DESTINATION CALL: an individually named, 30-year-designated holm oak with a real local story (the 360 sheep, the pastoral pruning, an information panel, an active 2025 tourism write-up), but modest in absolute size (8.5m tall) and, like Eraulgo artea, sitting alone in farmland rather than in any existing cluster: 26.1km from Bilbao (published), 71km from Eraulgo artea, 28.6km from Ondategiko Haritza (the closest of the four to it, but still outside a walkable or day-trip radius), 110.8km from Roble Escarcio. Recording the verified facts; the container decision (single-famous-tree exception, a future Durangaldea/Garai cluster, or staying a lead) is not mine to force.

CURATOR CALL, 2026-09-27: Recommend HOLD. No numeric age (only 'centenaria'), and the tree stands in a working farmhouse's meadow reached by an 800m track through someone's land; the tourism writeup invites visitors but this is thinner ground than the other four trees in this batch, which all carry either a real age figure or an unambiguous public access statement. Kept as a lead rather than a standalone place; would sit well in a future Durangaldea/Bizkaia cluster if other trees turn up nearby.

leads.name: Mesto de las Rozas
leads.blocked_reason: Known dead. This is Montalban de Cordoba's 'Mesto de las Rozas', a Quercus ilex x Quercus suber natural hybrid in the Las Rozas area (Campina Cordobesa), about 7km from the town (approx. municipality centre 37.5477, -4.7430; no tree-level coordinate exists or is needed now). es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesto_de_las_Rozas (fetched directly) states the trunk split and the whole crown fell in a severe storm in summer 1995; only the trunk and a regrowth shoot remain on site. The one photo we hold, File:Elmesto.jpg, is captioned on Commons 'El Mesto de las Rozas. Anos 80' (the tree in the 1980s), i.e. it depicts the tree BEFORE it fell, not a current living specimen; publishing it as a photo of a living tree would misrepresent a historical image as current. The brief's guess that 'Mesto' was an Asturias/Cantabria term was wrong; it is a Cordoba/Andalusia hybrid-oak name and this is a different region entirely from the other three candidates in this batch. Hard rule: never publish a tree known to be dead. This can appear only as historical context inside a story about the region, never as a collectible entry. Verification pass 2026-09-27.

page.intro: Until the Spanish Civil War, the village of Ondategi in Álava held its August festival under one oak, with one accordion for music. The Sarragoa oak, Ondategiko Haritza in Basque, is a pedunculate oak twenty metres tall with a crown about thirty metres across, standing on the communal meadow at the edge of the village. The Basque Government declared it a Singular Tree in 1997, one of ten in Álava. The festival did not survive the war; the oak did. Free, on the open meadow.
page.meta_description: Ondategiko Haritza, the Sarragoa oak: a pedunculate oak with a 30-metre crown where Ondategi held its festival. Free, on a communal meadow.
page.question_meta: Ondategiko Haritza is a protected pedunculate oak on the Sarragoa meadow in Ondategi, Álava, with a 30-metre crown. Its story and how to find it.
page.question_answer: Ondategiko Haritza, also called the Roble de Sarragoa, is a pedunculate oak on the campa of Sarragoa, the communal meadow at the southwest edge of Ondategi in the municipality of Zigoitia, Álava. It is about twenty metres tall with a crown around thirty metres wide and a trunk 4.9 metres round, and the Basque Government declared it a Singular Tree in 1997. It is free to visit on the open meadow.
page.question_context: The tree's best story is about a party. Ondategi's romería of San Lorenzo fell on 10 August, but the village could only afford paid musicians for one feast a year, Santa Lucía on 13 December. So in August the celebration took place in the shade of the Sarragoa oak with a single accordionist, and it went on that way until the Spanish Civil War, after which the romería under the tree was not revived. For generations the oak also gave shade and shelter to livestock and people on the meadow. It goes by several names: Ondategiko Haritza, Sarragoako haritza, the Roble de Sarragoa, and the plainest of them, the Árbol gordo de Zanagua, the fat tree. The Basque Government listed it as a Singular Tree in 1997, one of ten in the province of Álava, and the published measurement puts its trunk at 4.9 metres round at chest height. Every source calls it centenario, which means old and says nothing more precise. No one has published an age, and a reader who knows when the romería under it began would already be telling us more than any source does.

faq.a: No source gives an age. Every account calls it centenario, simply meaning very old. If you know more, tell us.

Until the Spanish Civil War, Ondategi held its August romería of San Lorenzo under its crown, with a single accordionist playing, because the village could afford paid musicians only for its December feast.
Yes. It stands on an open communal meadow at the edge of the village, with no gate or ticket.

Go to Ondategi, in the municipality of Zigoitia, Álava, and take the street to the left of the church to its end; the oak stands on the Sarragoa meadow. The village is about 13 kilometres from Vitoria-Gasteiz, and a car is the realistic way to get there.

tree_overrides.access: Free. Stands on an open communal meadow (campa) at the edge of the village, reached by the street that runs to the left of the church; no gate or ticket. Also known locally as the Roble de Sarragoa, Sarragoako haritza or the Árbol gordo de Zanagua.
tree_overrides.transport: Rural Zigoitia, Álava, about 13km from Vitoria-Gasteiz and 38km from Bilbao; there is no realistic public transport, so a car is the practical way to reach it.

page.intro: Dutch elm disease emptied the village squares of Alicante province of their elms, and in Millena, a village of around two hundred people in El Comtat, one is still standing. The field elm in front of the Church of Sant Josep is locally called the thousand-year elm, and is more likely two to three centuries old. Its trunk is 5.30 metres round, its heavy limbs propped on pillars after a snowfall broke one. The village signposts it at the entrance to town. Free, in the open church square.
page.meta_description: The Olmo centenario de Millena, a field elm 5.30 metres round, survives in the church square of a small Alicante village. Free, in the open square.
page.question_meta: The Olmo centenario de Millena is a field elm of roughly 200 to 300 years in the church square of Millena, Alicante. Its story and how to find it.
page.question_answer: The Olmo centenario de Millena, locally the Om mil·lenari, is a field elm in the Plaza de la Iglesia in front of the Church of Sant Josep in Millena, a small village in the El Comtat district of Alicante province. Published estimates put it at about 300 years, and possibly nearer 200. Its trunk is 5.30 metres round, and it is free to see in the open square.
page.question_context: Dutch elm disease killed most of the old village elms of this part of Spain, and two independent accounts describe Millena's as the last healthy one still standing in a plaza in the province. The local name, the thousand-year elm, overstates it considerably. Published estimates say about three hundred years, and one travel writer who visited suggests it may be younger still: elms were planted in Spanish town squares to mark the Cádiz Constitution of 1812, and he wonders whether this is one of them. That is his theory rather than a record, so the honest range is somewhere between two and three centuries. The measurements are firmer. The trunk is 5.30 metres round, the tree about ten metres tall with a crown up to eleven metres across. A limb broke under snow, pillars were put in to hold up the rest, and a later snowfall damaged one of the pillars. The elm is not on the Valencian catalogue of monumental trees, but it is protected under the region's 2006 law on monumental trees. The most recent account we found dates from 2016, so a current report from a visitor would be welcome.

faq.q: Is the elm really a thousand years old?
faq.a: No. The local name means the thousand-year elm, but published estimates put it at about 300 years, and one visitor's theory would make it nearer 200.

Dutch elm disease killed most of the old village elms of the region, and by two independent accounts this is the last healthy one still standing in a plaza in Alicante province. Its trunk is 5.30 metres round.
Yes. It stands in the open church square in the centre of Millena, and the village signposts it at the entrance to town.
Millena is in inland Alicante province, between Gorga and Cocentaina, and no public transport reaches it. Drive from Cocentaina or Alcoi; it is roughly 65 kilometres from Alicante city.

tree_overrides.transport: Rural inland Alicante province (El Comtat district), between Gorga and Cocentaina; no public transport reaches the village. Roughly 65km from Alicante city; most practical by car from Cocentaina or Alcoi.
